data.text/markdown:
The data: from the SQL export to one training row

This notebook follows a single object end to end and then shows what a batch of them looks like, so that every number the VAE consumes can be traced back to a column in the export. Two representations exist, and only one of them trains:
artifact built by holds used by
data/raw/miniJpas_fluxes_errors_redshifts_full.csv the archive 64,327 rows, 60 fluxes + 60 relative errors + metadata dataset.py only
data/interim/objects.parquet make interim one row per object: flux, absolute sigma, validity mask, metadata features, splits, modeling.data
data/interim/band_scales.parquet make interim per-band soft scale b_j features
data/interim/folds.parquet make splits leave-one-tile-out fold per object modeling.data, train, predict
data/processed/jpas_asinh.parquet make features exploratory asinh view: x, sigma_x, mask this notebook, tests
data/processed/vae_inputs.npz make model-data g, v, mask, logr, sig_logr, fold train.py, predict.py
models/vae.pt, reports/metrics.json make train weights, architecture, noise floor, history predict.py
data/processed/vae_latents.parquet make predict z_0..z_5, l_mu, reconstruction loss downstream analysis
The important structural fact: training never reads jpas_asinh.parquet. It reads vae_inputs.npz (jpas_da/modeling/data.py). Sections 1-5 describe the asinh view because it is how the flux is understood and checked; sections 6-10 describe the arrays that are actually optimised. Labels (zsp, zph, spCLASSsdss, photoCLASSsdss) and position/magnitude columns are carried in objects.parquet for inference and diagnostics and are never fed to the model.

1. The sample at a glance
objects 64,293
channels per object 60 (54 narrow + uJAVA + 4 broad + J1007)
tiles / folds 4 pointings, one leave-one-out fold each: 2241, 2243, 2406, 2470
objects with all 60 errors measured 60,991 (94.86%)
objects with at least one masked channel 3,302
masked pixels 38,916 (1.01%)
object id <tile_id>-<number>, e.g. 2241-2
folds present 4

How to load it

from jpas_da.modeling.data import load      # what training uses

a = load()                                  # data/processed/vae_inputs.npz
g, v, mask = a["g"], a["v"], a["mask"]      # (n_objects, 60) float32 / int8
logr, sig_logr = a["logr"], a["sig_logr"]   # (n_objects,)     float32
fold = a["fold"]                            # leave-one-tile-out assignment

from jpas_da.features import load_arrays    # the asinh view

b = load_arrays()                           # data/processed/jpas_asinh.parquet
x, sigma_x, mask = b["x"], b["sigma_x"], b["mask"]
Band order is the single definition in jpas_da.bands.BAND_NAMES, identical in every array, so no column matching can drift. load() refuses a file that is missing any of g, v, mask, logr, sig_logr, fold, object_id.

data.text/html:
2. The 60 channels

block n members role
narrow 54 J0378 ... J0910 the low-resolution spectrum, 10 nm step (J0378->J0390 is 12 nm)
medium 1 uJAVA 49.5 nm FWHM at 350 nm, the blue anchor
broad 4 uJPAS, gSDSS, rSDSS, iSDSS rSDSS is the detection band, far deeper than a narrow band
highpass 1 J1007 the red edge
894 nm of contiguous coverage in 60 channels. Adjacent narrow bands overlap, which is why the encoder is a 1-D convolution along this axis rather than a dense layer.

3. What dataset.py has to repair before anything else works

The export was written by an SQL query (its first line is the query itself) and is not analysis-ready. Measured on the shipped file:
defect count what the pipeline does
duplicated (tile_id, number) 34 keep the smallest angDist row; fluxes are identical within a group
e<band> == 0 (uncertainty not computed) 1.01% of pixels sigma = NaN, mask = 0
zsp < 0 / zph < 0 sentinels 193 / 813 NaN; zsp == 0 is kept only for STARs
MAGrSDSS > 30 sentinel 913 NaN
Rows: 64,327 -> 64,293 objects. The e<band> == 0 case is the dangerous one. Zero relative error reads as infinitely precise, but it means not computed: those pixels sit on faint sources in the noisiest bands, and unevenly across pointings:
tile objects with >=1 masked channel
2241 5.50%
2243 4.90%
2406 5.80%
2470 4.14%
build_photometry therefore produces sigma and mask together: sigma is NaN exactly where mask == 0, so the two can never disagree. An f/sigma representation would silently turn these pixels into enormous signal-to-noise; asinh plus an explicit mask cannot.sigma_f = |flux * FLUX_RELERR_AUTO|, because the export's error column is a signed relative error, not an absolute one. The flux unit is not uJy: the zeropoint is 26.1147, and MAGrSDSS is exactly 26.1147 - 2.5*log10(rSDSS), which is why it is kept out of every feature array.

data.text/markdown:
The transform, and its exact inverse

x       = asinh(f / b_j) * 2                     # exploratory view
sigma_x = sigma_f / sqrt(f^2 + b_j^2) * 2        # chain rule: d asinh(f/b)/df = 1/sqrt(f^2+b^2)
f       = b_j * sinh(x / 2)                      # exact inverse
Checked here, live: over the 3,818,664 measured pixels the maximum relative error of x -> f is 5.3e-07 (median 3.4e-08), i.e. float32 storage noise. features.build asserts the same thing on every rebuild. Masked pixels carry x = 0 and sigma_x = NaN and are excluded above: their x is 0 by construction, so inverting them would invent a flux. That is the reason the loss must be masked rather than the reconstruction trusted everywhere. The factor 2 (features.PRESENTATION_SCALE) is monotonic, so it changes no distance ordering; it exists so the channels have a convenient numerical size and so the file stays invertible.

data.text/html:
6. The uncertainty survives the transform

The error is propagated, not discarded: sigma_x is the flux error mapped through the same function as the flux.
  • in flux units the median error grows 4.6x from the faintest to the brightest decile;
  • in asinh units it varies only 1.7x over the nine faintest deciles, and drops on the brightest, where the data really are better.
That near-flatness is what a heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood wants: the noise model does not have to learn "trust bright pixels more", the sigma channel already says it.

data.text/markdown:
7. What the model actually optimises

The asinh view is for looking and checking. Training reads data/processed/vae_inputs.npz, built by jpas_da/modeling/data.py, which rewrites flux and error as a per-object brightness and a unit-norm shape: 
r        = sqrt( sum_j f_j^2 * m_j )                  brightness (masked bands excluded)
g_j      = f_j / r                                    SED shape, unit norm over m_j = 1
v_j      = sqrt( sigma_j^2 + (0.026 f_j)^2 ) / r      shape error, 0 where m_j = 0
logr     = log r                                      brightness target
sig_logr = sqrt( sum_j m_j g_j^2 v_j^2 )              its statistical error
Why this and not x:
  • The shape and the brightness are separate physical questions. A model of "what kind of object is this" should see g, not g * r; brightness is a distance/luminosity axis and gets its own scalar target.
  • Dividing flux and error by the same per-object scalar leaves every Gaussian likelihood term invariant, so this is conditioning, not modelling. It uses the object's own numbers only - no sample statistic - so it cannot leak across folds.
  • 0.026 is the survey's relative photometric-calibration scatter (~0.028 mag), a constant, not a fitted quantity.
  • A masked band gets g = 0, v = 0, so it contributes exactly zero to the loss instead of an invented uncertainty.
Note the one thing not stored here: the additive per-band error floor. It must be fitted on the training fold only, so train.py derives it at run time (section 11).

The invariants, checked

property measured expected
sqrt(sum(g^2 * mask)) 1.000000 .. 1.000000 1.0
v where masked 0.0 0
v where measured p1 0.0036, median 0.0617, p99 0.2413 > 0
logr p1 3.53, median 4.94, p99 10.10 log of a positive norm
sig_logr median 0.116, p99 0.217 > 0
r spans 21582348x across the sample, and logr puts that on an additive scale. v is the same quantity as sigma_x from section 6, just measured relative to the object's own brightness instead of to the band's depth.

A warning that shapes every later result

Split the shape channel into an overall level and a per-band deviation from it:
component share of variance in g
per-object level (mean of g) 12%
per-band shape (colour) 89%
A large fraction of g's variance is still a single number per object: how much of the total flux sits in the mean band versus the edges. That is why a very small latent can already reconstruct a lot, and why the reconstruction number must always be compared with the "predict the sample mean" baseline (section 12) rather than taken at face value.

11. Splits: leave one pointing out

fold held-out tile validation objects training objects
0 2241 20,016 44,277
1 2243 13,836 50,457
2 2406 15,792 48,501
3 2470 14,649 49,644
The unit of independence is the pointing, not the object. Objects are never shared between the four miniJPAS pointings, but neighbours inside one pointing share sky background, crowding and a common photometric calibration. A random row split would train and score on the same noise. The pointings also differ in depth, so a fold score is partly a depth-mismatch score. That is the intended reading - it is the production situation, applying a model to a new field. 
train, val = np.flatnonzero(fold != k), np.flatnonzero(fold == k)

data.text/html:
12. The noise floor, and why v alone is not enough

The archive's error is purely relative, so v shrinks with the flux and a near-zero-flux band would claim infinite precision. The pipeline therefore adds a fixed per-band floor s_j, a low percentile of v computed on the training rows of the current fold only and then frozen: 
s_j = percentile(v[mask == 1, j][train_rows], 5)
w   = sqrt(v^2 + s_j^2)      # the variance the likelihood uses
Here s_j ranges 0.0044 .. 0.0296, i.e. 19% of a typical band's v. It is never learned: it is a property of the instrument, and fitting it on all folds would leak the held-out tile's noise level into the model. Note also that the floor is not in vae_inputs.npz. That is deliberate - a stored floor would be a floor fitted on every object, including the held-out tile. It is written into models/vae.pt after training so predict.py uses the same one.

data.text/markdown:
### Checking the checkpoint against the data it was trained on

    `models/vae.pt` currently on disk is a **debug** run (`make train-debug`),
    2 epoch(s), channels `['g', 'v', 'mask']`,
    latent width 6.

    | | masked RMSE of `g` |
    |---|---|
    | decoder, training folds | 0.1637 |
    | decoder, held-out fold | 0.1651 |
    | "predict the training-mean shape", held-out fold | 0.1205 |

    The decoder is **worse than the mean-shape baseline**. Latent spread per dimension:
    0.049, 0.041, 0.079, 0.021, 0.011, 0.027.

    Correlation of each latent with brightness: `z_0` +0.05, `z_1` +0.01, `z_2` -0.02, `z_3` +0.05, `z_4` +0.20, `z_5` +0.04.

    Read this as a pipeline check, not a result: two epochs cannot beat a
one-parameter baseline, and the near-flat latent spread says the posterior has barely moved off its prior. If this cell shows the decoder ahead of the baseline after a real make train, the setup is sound.

13. What must not go in, and the guarantees the pipeline makes

do not feed why
MAGrSDSS exactly 26.1147 - 2.5*log10(rSDSS); a duplicate of a channel
angDist non-null exactly on the SDSS-cross-matched rows: encodes label availability
zsp, zph, avg_zph, e_* the labels the model is meant to help predict
spCLASSsdss, photoCLASSsdss same
ALPHA_J2000, DELTA_J2000, flag_rSDSS position and selection, not photometry
All of them stay in objects.parquet so downstream inference can join them back on object_id.
requirement enforced by
no NaN in any model channel model_data.normalise raises on non-finite g/v/logr
v == 0 exactly where mask == 0 constructed that way, asserted in tests/test_data.py
g unit-norm over measured bands np.sqrt((g^2 * mask).sum(1)) == 1, checked above
canonical band order one definition, jpas_da.bands.BAND_NAMES
exact invertibility of the asinh view features.check_roundtrip on every build
fold assignment covers every object model_data.build raises otherwise
floor fitted on training rows only train.noise_floor receives train_index
checkpoint cannot be loaded into a different architecture build_model takes every value explicitly from the checkpoint

Reading the rest of the project

  • vae-normalisation-and-loss.md - derivations and measurements behind the normalisation and each loss term.
  • jpas_da/modeling/data.py - the RMS decomposition, in ~50 lines.
  • jpas_da/modeling/train.py - floor, KL warm-up, brightness head, checkpoint.
  • data/processed/vae_latents.parquet - what make predict writes; start any analysis from there rather than re-running the network.
